Summary Candidates should listen to the recording very carefully and develop techniques and strategies to enable them to identify and select appropriate details for their answers. There is a need to work on emerging Hindi vocabulary to access some questions and also to focus on sounds and letters, paying particular attention to similar-sounding letters. Teachers should also try dictation activities with their candidates regularly in class. Candidates should gain as much practice as possible at listening exercises or news in class and attempt past papers under timed conditions. All this would certainly help to raise the overall standard. HINDI AS A

Paper 2 In order to do well in this examination, candidates should: • Write their answers as clearly as possible so that the meaning can be understood. • Take care to include all the relevant details in their answers to the questions in Exercise 3. Overall, candidates performed quite well in this examination and the full range of ability was observed. Most candidates attempted all the questions in the paper. For this component, credit is given for communication of the correct information. Answers are not assessed for accuracy of spelling and grammar. However, if language errors change the meaning or the meaning is unclear, the answer cannot be given credit. Comments on specific questions Exercise 1 Questions 1 – 6 The majority of candidates performed reasonably well on this exercise. Questions 1 – 6 require short answers, and most candidates fared well. There were variations in the spelling of some words. Some of the words are part of basic vocabulary and candidates are expected to be able to spell them correctly. Marks were awarded if the misspelled word did not change the meaning, but not for answers where it changed the meaning such as, for example, instead of ‘arth shaastra’ the candidate wrote ‘art shstra’.
notes.key_messages: • In order to access full marks, it is important for candidates to read the questions and stimulus material carefully and complete all the instructions given with the question. • The rubric of the question should be adhered to. It includes the word limit put on the question. The length of a ‘note’ should not be the same as an extended piece of continuous writing. A summary should extract the main points of a text excluding the detailed descriptions within it. • Candidates should know how to respond to ‘how’ and ‘why’ questions separately, answering only one of them will not give them access to full marks. • Candidates should use the mark allocation written in brackets at the end of each question as a guide. The mark allocation indicates the number of relevant points that need to be made in an answer. In some questions the number of responses required is stated in the question. Responding to them appropriately will secure full marks. • Some questions require answers in a single word/phrase (Questions 1 – 6) and others need to be answered in complete sentences (Questions 3 – 5). Candidates should avoid repeating the information given in the question. • Candidates are not penalised for awkward spelling, but the answers cannot be ambiguous. Spelling errors are tolerated only if the meaning is clear. • In some questions (Questions 3 – 5) Language marks are allocated separately. In order to access language marks, appropriate use of vocabulary, punctuation, paragraphing and register are essential.
notes.general_comments: Candidates are generally well prepared for the Reading and Writing examination. They are able to engage with the topics. Their responses mostly show their understanding of the text. Some of the weaker candidates struggled to provide precise responses to the questions and copied from the text. Correct grammatical structures and spelling errors compromise the quality of responses.
